card.law_is_about: Implementing the revised German greenhouse-gas emissions trading law through detailed monitoring and administration rules.
card.they_want: Exempt hazardous-waste incineration from the national carbon market or suspend that market until ETS 2 operates reliably.
card.they_claim: Waste-incineration carbon costs arise exclusively in Germany.
card.the_problem: Danish official guidance expressly imposes a CO₂ tax on relevant hazardous-waste incineration from 2015. That qualifies the Germany-only carbon-cost premise, while scope and net burdens still differ.

correction: Distinguish the absence of uniform EU-wide carbon pricing from the existence of national carbon costs elsewhere. The explicitly versioned Danish Tax Agency 2026-1 guidance states that relevant hazardous-waste incineration has been subject to CO₂ tax since 1 January 2015, while separately explaining its ETS exclusion. Its calculation chapter covers non-biodegradable waste used for heat/electricity, with material and use-based exemptions. Thus carbon charges on relevant hazardous incineration were not exclusive to Germany. Earlier Danish/Swedish waste-to-energy ETS evidence is corroborating background, not the sole matched-cohort counterexample.
effect: Qualifies the premise of a uniquely German carbon-cost burden supporting removal or suspension of national pricing. It does not eliminate possible differences in coverage, rates, exemptions, compensation or competitive disadvantage.
limits: The correction establishes foreign carbon taxation of relevant hazardous-waste incineration, not that every dedicated destruction plant is charged. Danish rules are limited by energy/heat use, non-biodegradable content and exemptions; a pure-destruction or exempt-material case may differ. No equal net cost, no quantified foreign tax payment and no absence of a German competitive burden is asserted. Dedicated hazardous sites can be outside ETS while within a separate carbon tax. Possible state compensation and the incidence of heat-related charges remain distinct from the existence of the tax. No policy-merit or intent conclusion follows.
context_and_alternatives: Both author pages were read. The challenged sentence follows a reference to waste-incineration plants newly covered by BEHG and precedes the dedicated hazardous-waste discussion. The request offers both a targeted exemption and broad BEHG suspension.

The first independent review correctly withheld a finding because ordinary energy-recovery ETS examples might not match the implicit dedicated hazardous-waste cohort. New affirmative Danish hazardous-waste CO₂ tax guidance changes that evidentiary basis. Both assessments are retained in the review history.

An instrument-specific reading could mean only Germany has the German BEHG, or only Germany added this particular charge in 2024. That is a plausible narrower description, but the printed causal argument refers to missing European pricing and says additional costs arise exclusively in Germany. The narrow correction concerns carbon-cost uniqueness, not uniqueness of the German statutory instrument or identical implementation dates.

The Danish minister’s 2022 response separately identifies specialised hazardous-waste incineration/destruction facilities. It corroborates the dedicated cohort, but its proposed future rates and support are not treated as proof of actual paid sums, current compensation or individual net burdens.

The tax guide 2026-1 historical edition was retrieved using explicit vid220619. An earlier bare-URL local download actually selected 2026-2 although the web reader displayed 2026-1. The registry now cites the historical archive; the old file remains preserved and is not represented as pre-submission evidence.

Exact January consultation draft and ministry record were checked; later July regulation is not substituted. Future 2028 waste-sector extension in the author is treated as a proposal, not a proved timetable error.

The guide carries a historical 2026-1 edition identifier, but its webpage can automatically append later decisions, including a February 2026 case. Those later case listings are not used as pre-author evidence. The cited main historical text describes the 2015 tax rule; the HTML is not represented as a frozen January 2026 snapshot.
materiality_explanation: Minor: a supporting international-uniqueness premise is overstated. The correction does not quantify relative costs or settle the broader competitive burden, and independent implementation objections remain.
direction_explanation: True narrowly: exclusive German carbon costs support a targeted exemption or broad suspension. Affirmative foreign hazardous-waste carbon taxation qualifies that premise; this direction is separate from the minor materiality assessment.

confidence.text_source_mismatch: High for affirmative foreign hazardous-waste carbon-tax rules; energy use, exemptions and net-cost differences limit the scope of the correction.
